claim: In a 2021 study of 30 dietary supplements purchased on Amazon, only 13 of 30 had accurate labels; 13 had ingredients listed that were not in the product, 9 had unlisted ingredients, and none had third-party certification seals.
stance_target: Amazon supplements carry significant mislabeling and quality risks
scope_conditions: 30 dietary supplements purchased on Amazon, 2021 study
quoted_support: In 2021, an evaluation of 30 dietary supplements purchased on Amazon was carried out, and only 13 of the 30 were found to have accurate labels. Of the remaining 17 with inaccurate labels, 13 of them had ingredients listed on the label that weren't found in the product itself. Nine of the 17 had ingredients detected in them that weren't listed on the product label. None of the 30 products tested had third-party certification seals on their packaging.

claim: E-commerce represents 15% of the total supplement market, with 77% of those online supplement sales occurring through Amazon.
stance_target: Amazon's dominance in online supplement sales
quoted_support: A 2022 article estimates that eCommerce represents 15% of the total supplement market, with 77% of supplement sales happening through Amazon.
numbers: 15% of total supplement market is eCommerce
77% of supplement eCommerce sales on Amazon

claim: Fraudulent sellers on Amazon can pass third-party verification testing by submitting legitimate products while continuing to sell counterfeit versions to customers.
stance_target: Amazon's supplement safety verification process has a critical loophole
scope_conditions: Amazon's supplement verification policy as of April 2024
quoted_support: Since the product samples are sent by the sellers to the third-party verifiers for testing rather than being sent by Amazon directly from their warehouses, this can create a conflict of interest. Fraudulent sellers could send a legitimate product for testing but continue to actually sell counterfeit products to customers.
numbers: As of April 8, 2024: Eurofins, NSF International, UL Solutions approved as Amazon verifiers

claim: NOW Foods discovered 11 different counterfeit NOW supplement products (including psyllium husk, magnesium citrate, and men's multivitamin) being sold on Amazon by a single fraudulent seller in 2023.
stance_target: Even established, well-known supplement brands are counterfeited on Amazon
quoted_support: NOW Foods discovered 11 different counterfeit NOW supplements, including psyllium husk capsules, magnesium citrate, and a men's multivitamin, sold on Amazon by a single Amazon seller.

claim: Amazon only mandatorily verifies supplement quality for sexual enhancement, weight management, and sports/bodybuilding categories — not for general vitamins and minerals like Vitamin D3.
stance_target: Vitamin D3 supplements on Amazon face minimal mandatory quality verification
scope_conditions: Amazon seller policy as of April 2024
quoted_support: Amazon requires sellers to verify that supplement products in the sexual enhancement, weight management, and sports/bodybuilding categories meet Amazon's policy via third-party testing and document verification on an annual basis.
